claims.text: Applying plasma-assisted nitriding to boride-based components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
A BN surface layer impedes aluminum infiltration and reaction with the boride substrate.
Standard boriding treatments produce boride surface layers.
A nitrogen-rich plasma treatment at approximately 900 °C for 2–4 hours and 10−2–10−3 mbar will form a homogeneous BN layer 3–5 µm thick.
The resulting BN layer will be dense, uniform, and act as a diffusion barrier.
BN is chemically stable and inert at the relevant high temperatures.
The BN layer slows diffusion of aluminum into the boride substrate.
Slowing aluminum diffusion inhibits corrosive reactions and substrate degradation during prolonged molten-aluminum exposure.
Plasma-nitrided components will have a significantly lower corrosion rate than untreated boride-based components in molten aluminum.
Plasma-nitrided components will retain better structural integrity than untreated boride-based components in molten aluminum.
The comparison baseline is a standard boride-based component without the BN barrier treatment.
Effectiveness depends on the BN layer retaining a uniform thickness of 3–5 µm and remaining adherent during thermal cycling.
The intervention's benefits are limited to environments near 900 °C.
Temperatures near 900 °C are typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating processes.
Repeated thermal cycling and mechanical stress may degrade or delaminate the BN layer and reduce its barrier properties over extended operation.
